podcast.title: R.E.M.'s Departure (1987)
podcast.body: R.E.M. concluded their tenure with IRS Records after the release of their 1987 album *Document*, moving on to Warner Music. This transition was prompted by unspecified "problems and certain disagreements" that arose between the band and the independent label. "justo después por si otros problemas y ciertos asenfados con la discográfica se pasaría a Warner."

podcast.title: Bankruptcy Impact on Head
podcast.body: IRS Records, known for signing bands like R.E.M. and Head, eventually went bankrupt, which directly caused Head to founder and break up after a couple more years. "But then IRS went bankrupt and the band started to founder and after a couple of more years they broke up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Challenges for Indie Labels and Bands
podcast.body: Most indie labels often faced difficulties in consistently getting music into stores, and even when they did, bands had trouble getting paid. This financial instability and limited distribution often necessitated constant touring for bands like R.E.M. to gain exposure and make ends meet. "Most indie labels have a very hard time getting music into the stores on a consistent and regular basis."

podcast.title: Discovery of R.E.M.
podcast.body: IRS Records was a small independent record label that gained historical notoriety for being the company that discovered and signed R.E.M. in the early 1980s, notably being the sole entity that initially showed interest in the band. R.E.M. maintained a close working relationship with IRS, releasing numerous albums with them up until 1987, concluding with the album *Document*. "sería una pequeña discográfica independiente, IRS Records, que pasaría la historia por ser la discográfica que descubrió a rem, la única que se entera sería por ellos."

podcast.title: Indie Label and R.E.M.'s Growth
podcast.body: IRS Records was a larger indie label run by Miles Copeland, brother of Police drummer Stuart Copeland. R.E.M. released five albums on IRS between 1982 and 1985, growing to be one of North America's most respected alternative bands and pioneers of the college rock scene. However, by 1987, R.E.M. outgrew IRS's distribution and support capabilities, leading to their departure for a major label. "IRS distribution, their ability to get R.E.M. records into record stores, had gone as far as it could, and it was time to move on to someone who could get the records out there worldwide."

podcast.title: Interest in Hassel Adkins
podcast.body: Miles Copeland, the head of IRS Records and brother of Stuart Copeland of The Police, expressed interest in producing an album with Hassel Adkins, although the project ultimately did not materialize. "Miles Copeland, the head of IRS records, brother of Stuart Copeland of the police, wanted to do an album with him, but it never worked out."

podcast.title: Leonard Cohen's Relaunch
podcast.body: In 1988, IRS Records made the decision to launch or relaunch Leonard Cohen's career by marketing him as an alternative artist, coinciding with the release of his album *I'm Your Man*. "For some reason, IRS records had decided to launch or relaunch Leonard Cohen's career as an alternative artist."
